sections.h2: What a Georgia transfer on death deed is
sections.html:
A transfer on death deed, often shortened to TOD deed, lets a Georgia owner name who gets a piece of real estate after the owner dies, without a separate transfer during life. The rules sit in Chapter 17 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia, Code Sections 44-17-1 through 44-17-7. The chapter first took effect on July 1, 2024 under SB 420, and HB 413 rewrote parts of it effective April 22, 2026.

The deed is recorded while the owner is alive, but it does nothing to the owner's rights until death. Under Code Section 44-17-7, the owner stays the legal and equitable owner and counts as an absolute owner with regard to creditors and purchasers. A house under a TOD deed can still be sold, mortgaged or leased by the owner without asking the person named in the deed.

sections.h2: Who can sign and what the deed needs
sections.html:
Only the record owner can sign it, and that owner needs the same legal capacity required to enter into a contract. An attorney in fact acting under a power of attorney is not authorized to sign one. Code Section 44-17-2 says the deed needs no consideration, so no payment has to change hands.

The deed is recorded with the clerk of superior court in the county where the land sits. A few points from the current text of Section 44-17-2:

  • The person named is called a grantee beneficiary, and the owner may name one or several.
  • The owner may name alternate beneficiaries who take only if a primary beneficiary dies first or dies before accepting the property.
  • A trustee of an express trust may be named as the beneficiary.
  • The deed cannot be used to create an express trust or a beneficial interest in real property under the trust code articles the statute cites.
  • No signature, consent or notice to the beneficiary is required while the owner is alive.
  • A real estate transfer tax declaration form is not filed with the deed itself.

sections.h2: Changing or cancelling a TOD deed
sections.html:
You can revoke or replace it at any time before death, and the beneficiary does not have to agree. Section 44-17-4 sets two routes: record a revocation instrument, or record a later TOD deed. A later deed wipes out every earlier beneficiary designation for the same interest.

A revocation must refer to the original deed, carry the owner's signature, and have that signature attested by an officer as provided in Code Section 44-2-15 plus one other witness. Before the 2026 amendment the statute asked for two other witnesses, and an attorney in fact could also sign it. A will cannot revoke a recorded TOD deed, so a clause in a will naming someone else does not override it.

Selling the property during life ends the deed as well. Section 44-17-4(d) says that if the owner sells or conveys the interest, or moves it into the owner's own express trust, the TOD deed is revoked. It is also revoked if the only named beneficiary dies before accepting.

sections.h2: What happens to the house when the owner dies?
sections.html:
The beneficiary must take two steps after the death, and the title does not pass until both are complete. First, each beneficiary who wants the property signs an affidavit. Second, the affidavit is recorded. The property is not handed over automatically on the date of death.

The affidavit must verify the owner's death, say whether the owner and the beneficiary were married at the time of death, give the deed book and page of the recorded TOD deed, and include a legal description of the land. A copy of the death certificate is attached. For an owner who dies on or after July 1, 2026, the beneficiary records the affidavit, the real estate transfer tax declaration form and related papers with the clerk of superior court of the county where the land is located.

The earlier version of the statute gave beneficiaries nine months to record or the interest reverted to the estate. Section 44-17-2(e) no longer contains that deadline. Ask the clerk of superior court or a Georgia real estate attorney how a particular death date is handled, because the recording rule is tied to deaths on or after July 1, 2026.

sections.h2: The TOD deed process step by step
sections.html:
From signing to title passing, the order runs like this.

Georgia TOD deed steps
StepWhat happensCode section
Sign and record the deedRecord owner signs; recorded with the clerk of superior court; no consideration needed44-17-2(a)
Change courseRecord a revocation (officer plus one witness) or a later TOD deed44-17-4(a), (b)
Owner diesPersonal representative gives each beneficiary notice as under Code Section 53-5-844-17-2(g)(1)
Beneficiary acceptsExecute the affidavit, attach the death certificate, record it44-17-2(c) to (e)
Title passesProperty moves to the beneficiary subject to recorded liens and mortgages44-17-5(a)

sections.h2: Selling a house under a TOD deed
sections.html:
A sale can happen at two different stages, and the paperwork differs. While the owner is alive, the owner sells as usual and signs the deed to the buyer, which revokes the TOD deed under Section 44-17-4(d).

After the death, the beneficiary can sell only once the acceptance affidavit is recorded, because that step moves the title out of the estate. A beneficiary who inherits a house with repairs, back taxes or a mortgage balance often wants a quick closing. We buy houses in Georgia as-is for cash, which can fit when the beneficiary lives out of town and does not want to manage a vacant property.

If the beneficiary has not accepted, the estate still holds the property. A personal representative of an insolvent estate that faces imminent foreclosure, condemnation or destruction may record an affidavit of notice with the lender's or government's notice attached. If no beneficiary has completed the acceptance steps, the representative can then sell the property, pay the debts, and return any remaining proceeds to the estate.

sections.h2: Who still has a claim on the house?
sections.html:
The beneficiary takes the house subject to every recorded mortgage, lien, lease, easement and security deed that the owner made or was bound by. Section 44-17-5(a) lists recorded executory contracts of sale and options to purchase among them, and it covers any interest the owner conveyed that was smaller than the whole. A nonconsensual lien against the beneficiary does not attach until the acceptance affidavit is recorded.

Two points work in the beneficiary's favor. A person who became the owner's spouse after the TOD deed was signed cannot claim against it. The deed also takes priority over the unsecured debts of the owner's estate filed after death, unless the property is unredeemed.

  • Mortgage lenders keep their recorded security deeds.
  • Property tax liens stay ahead of the estate's repair lien described below.
  • A spouse who married the owner before the deed was signed is not cut off by the later-spouse rule.

sections.h2: If a beneficiary dies first or the estate pays the bills
sections.html:
If one of several beneficiaries dies before the owner, that share lapses and is split evenly among the surviving beneficiaries instead of going back to the estate. The same split applies to a beneficiary who dies after the owner but before accepting. If the deed names joint tenants with right of survivorship, a beneficiary's earlier death does not invalidate the joint tenancy for the others.

While the property waits for acceptance, a personal representative of a solvent estate may pay the mortgage, property taxes and repairs needed to keep the house from being destroyed. The estate is entitled to repayment and gets a priority special lien for any amount still unpaid one year after the beneficiary accepts. That lien is inferior to property tax liens and earlier recorded security deeds, and the estate has 30 days after the one-year mark to file a claim of lien with the clerk of superior court.

faqs.q: Is a transfer on death deed legal in Georgia?
faqs.a: Yes. Georgia allows TOD deeds for real estate under O.C.G.A. 44-17-1 through 44-17-7, in effect since July 1, 2024 and amended by HB 413 effective April 22, 2026.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to sign the TOD deed?
faqs.a: No. No signature, consent, agreement or notice to the beneficiary is required while the record owner is alive. The beneficiary signs only the acceptance affidavit after the owner's death.

faqs.q: Can a will override a TOD deed in Georgia?
faqs.a: No. A recorded TOD deed may not be revoked by the provisions of a will. The owner must record a revocation or a new TOD deed.

faqs.q: Where is the deed or affidavit recorded?
faqs.a: With the clerk of superior court in the county where the real estate is located. Ask that clerk's office for its recording requirements and fees.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited Georgia house before the affidavit is recorded?
faqs.a: Not as the beneficiary. Until acceptance is complete the property is still handled through the estate. Ask a Georgia probate or real estate attorney who can sign for the sale in your situation.
